questions.title: Plane dividing the body into a large right and a small left part
questions.question: The plane that divides the body into a large right part & a small left part is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The median plane runs exactly through the midline and divides the body into two equal right and left halves, not a large and a small part.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A plane offset to the right of the median line removes a thin slice from the right side, leaving a large left part and a small right part -- the mirror image of what this stem describes.
explanations.C: Correct. A parasagittal plane runs parallel and close to the median plane, so it always produces one large and one small half rather than two equal halves. A plane to the left of the median line removes only a thin slice from the left side, leaving a large right part and a small left part -- the exact division this stem describes. This is the same plane class tested from the opposite direction elsewhere in this set: planes are distinguished by the two parts each one leaves behind, not merely by whether they run vertically.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The coronal (frontal) plane is vertical but runs at right angles to the median plane, dividing the body into anterior and posterior parts, not right and left.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The transverse (horizontal) plane divides the body into upper and lower parts, not right and left.

questions.learning_objective: Name the anatomical plane described by a given right/left division of the body.

questions.title: Structure responsible for bone growth in length
questions.question: Which of the following is responsible for the growth of the bone in length?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The periosteum is responsible for growth in diameter (width), not length -- its osteoblasts lay down new bone on the outer surface of the shaft.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The endosteum lines the medullary cavity and is involved in internal remodelling and repair, not in lengthening the bone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The epiphysis is the expanded bony end itself, not the growth-producing cartilage -- that role belongs specifically to the epiphyseal plate within it.
explanations.D: Correct. A long bone increases in length by proliferation of the cartilage cells within its epiphyseal plates, one near each end of the shaft. As these cartilage cells divide and are progressively replaced by bone on the diaphyseal side, the shaft is pushed further from the two epiphyses, lengthening the whole bone. This is the growth-in-length mechanism, distinct from growth in width, which instead comes from the periosteum -- the pairing tested by a companion question in this same set.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The diaphysis is the shaft that lengthens as a result of growth, not the structure that drives the lengthening.

questions.learning_objective: Name the structure responsible for a long bone's growth in length.

questions.title: Bone type of the lunate
questions.question: What is the type of the lunate (carpal) bone?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Long bones have two expanded ends and a shaft, a form the lunate -- a small carpal bone -- does not have.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sesamoid bones are small nodules embedded within a tendon, such as the patella or the pisiform; the lunate is a true carpal bone of the wrist row, not a tendon nodule.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pneumatic bones contain air cavities, as in the skull bones around the nose; the lunate has no such air spaces.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Flat bones are two thin plates of compact bone around a spongy layer, as in the scapula or skull cap -- a different internal structure from the lunate's uniformly spongy short-bone build.
explanations.E: Correct. Bones are classified by shape into six classes, and the carpal bones -- including the lunate -- belong to the short-bone class: spongy bone under a thin shell of compact bone, roughly cuboidal in shape. The lunate sits in the proximal row of the carpus, between the scaphoid and the triquetrum, and like every other carpal bone it is a short bone regardless of its individual size or crescent shape. Size and shape of the whole bone do not decide the classification -- what matters is the internal spongy-under-a-thin-shell structure common to every short bone.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the lunate as a short bone by its shape.

questions.title: What the parasagittal plane divides the body into
questions.question: The parasagittal plane divides the body into:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Right and left equal halves describe the median plane, not a parasagittal one -- a parasagittal plane is by definition offset from the midline.
explanations.B: Correct. By definition a parasagittal plane is any plane parallel to, but offset from, the true median plane. Because it is offset, it can never bisect the body exactly, so it always divides the body into unequal right and left parts -- a large part on the side away from the offset and a small part on the side of the offset. This unequal-halves property is exactly what distinguishes a parasagittal plane from the median plane itself, the one vertical sagittal plane in this set that does give equal halves.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Anterior and posterior parts describe the coronal plane, which runs at right angles to a parasagittal plane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Upper and lower parts, whether equal or unequal, describe the transverse (horizontal) plane, not a parasagittal one.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Upper and lower unequal parts still describes a transverse-type division, not the right/left division a parasagittal plane gives.

questions.learning_objective: State that a parasagittal plane gives unequal right and left halves.

questions.title: Direction of toe adduction
questions.question: Adduction of toes occurs in which direction?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The middle toe is not the foot's reference axis for toe movements; that role belongs specifically to the second toe.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Away from the big toe describes neither adduction nor abduction correctly with respect to the true reference axis, the second toe.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Towards the big toe would describe abduction of a toe lateral to it relative to the second-toe axis, not adduction.
explanations.D: Correct. Unlike the hand, where finger abduction and adduction are described relative to the middle (third) finger, the foot uses the second toe as its reference axis, because the second toe lies on the long axis of the foot. Adduction of a toe is therefore movement towards the second toe, and abduction is movement away from it -- the toe-equivalent of the hand's middle-finger rule, but built around a different digit. This swapped reference axis is a common source of error for students who default to the hand's own convention.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Towards the midline of the body" is the hip-level term, as in adduction of the whole limb, not the toe-level convention, which uses the second toe as its own local axis.

questions.learning_objective: State that toe adduction/abduction is described relative to the second toe, not the middle toe.

questions.title: Clavicle as a long bone
questions.question: Which of the following is a long bone?

explanations.A: Correct. A long bone is defined by having two expanded ends and a shaft between them, and the clavicle fits this shape despite its unusual double curve and its horizontal, rather than vertical, orientation. It is the standing exception examiners return to because, although shaped like a long bone, the clavicle ossifies in membrane rather than from a cartilage model -- a point tested separately elsewhere in this set. Shape decides the "long bone" classification here; the way it ossifies is a separate, independent fact about the same bone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The vertebra is classified as an irregular bone because of its complex shape with projecting processes, not as a long bone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sternum is a flat bone -- two thin plates of compact bone around a spongy layer -- not a long bone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The maxilla is an irregular bone of the facial skeleton, not a long bone.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The scapula is a flat bone, not a long bone, despite lying within the upper limb skeleton.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the clavicle as a long bone by shape.

questions.title: Structure responsible for bone growth in diameter
questions.question: Which part of the bone is responsible for its growth in diameter (width)?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The primary centre of ossification is where a bone first turns from cartilage into bone before birth, not the structure that widens an already-formed long bone.
explanations.B: Correct. The inner (osteogenic) layer of the periosteum contains osteoblasts that lay down new bone circumferentially on the outer surface of the shaft, so the bone increases in diameter (width) as it grows. This is the width-growth partner to the epiphyseal plate's length-growth role: a long bone lengthens at its epiphyseal plates and widens from its periosteum. Confusing the two roles, or answering "epiphyseal plate" here, is the trap this question is built to catch.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The endosteum lines the inner (medullary) surface of the bone and is involved in remodelling that surface, not in adding bone to the outer diameter.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The epiphyseal plate lengthens the bone; it does not widen the shaft.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The metaphysis is the highly active region of the shaft just under the epiphyseal plate -- a site of active remodelling, not itself the structure responsible for width growth.

questions.learning_objective: Name the structure responsible for a long bone's growth in diameter.

questions.title: Site of thick skin
questions.question: The epidermis of the skin is thick in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The eyelids carry some of the thinnest skin in the body, the opposite of a thick-skin site.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The front of the arm is covered by ordinary thin (hairy) skin, not thick skin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The dorsum (back) of the hand is thin skin; only the palm (the opposite surface) is thick skin.
explanations.D: Correct. Thick (glabrous) skin is confined to the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet, where a markedly thickened epidermis -- with a distinct stratum lucidum not found in thin skin -- withstands the heavy friction and pressure of grip and weight-bearing. Every other site listed here is covered by thin (hairy) skin, the type that covers most of the body surface. This palm/sole-only distribution is the single fact that separates thick from thin skin anatomically.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The skin of the chest is thin (hairy) skin, not thick skin.

questions.learning_objective: Name the sites of thick (glabrous) skin.

questions.title: Bone that ossifies from a membrane
questions.question: A bone that ossifies from a membrane:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The scapula, like almost the whole limb skeleton, ossifies endochondrally from a cartilage model, not from a membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The hip bone ossifies endochondrally, from cartilage, not intramembranously.
explanations.C: Correct. Bone forms by one of two processes: directly within a connective-tissue membrane (intramembranous ossification) or by first forming a cartilage model that is then replaced by bone (endochondral ossification). The clavicle is the standing exception among the long bones -- shaped like a long bone, yet it ossifies intramembranously, alongside the bones of the skull vault, rather than from a cartilage model like the rest of the limb skeleton. This split between shape and mode of ossification is exactly what this question tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The base of the skull ossifies endochondrally from a cartilage model -- it is the skull vault (cap), not the base, that ossifies in membrane alongside the clavicle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The patella, a sesamoid bone, ossifies endochondrally from cartilage, not from a membrane.

questions.learning_objective: Name the clavicle as the long bone that ossifies intramembranously.

questions.title: Joint classification of the epiphyseal plate
questions.question: The epiphyseal plate of cartilage is:

explanations.A: Correct. A primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis) unites two bones by hyaline cartilage, is usually temporary, ossifies as growth completes, and allows no movement -- and the epiphyseal plate, uniting the epiphysis to the diaphysis by a disc of hyaline cartilage until it fuses, is the standard type example. This contrasts with a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis), which unites bones by fibrocartilage, lies in the midline, and is permanent, such as the pubic symphysis or the intervertebral discs. Classifying the epiphyseal plate as a joint at all, rather than simply as "growth cartilage", is the point this question tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A fibrous joint unites bones by fibrous tissue with no cartilage at all, such as a suture; the epiphyseal plate is cartilaginous, not fibrous.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A secondary cartilaginous joint is fibrocartilaginous and permanent, such as the pubic symphysis -- the opposite profile from the temporary hyaline-cartilage epiphyseal plate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A plane synovial joint has a joint cavity and synovial membrane, structures the epiphyseal plate does not have.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A hinge synovial joint, like the elbow, is a freely mobile synovial joint, unlike the immobile cartilaginous epiphyseal plate.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the epiphyseal plate as a primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis).

questions.title: Site where superficial fascia has no fat
questions.question: Superficial fascia is devoid of fat at:

explanations.A: Correct. Superficial fascia is a layer of loose connective tissue deep to the skin that normally carries a variable amount of fat, but at a small number of named sites it contains no fat at all -- the eyelids, the penis and the scrotum are the classic examples. This absence of fat is functionally important: at the eyelids it keeps the lid thin and mobile enough for rapid, repeated blinking, which a fat-laden superficial fascia would hinder. The other options are all sites where superficial fascia is normal or even fat-rich, the opposite of what the stem asks for.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The thigh is one of the sites where superficial fascia contains an abundant quantity of fat, not one where fat is absent.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The arm carries a normal amount of fat within its superficial fascia; fat is not characteristically absent there.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The back of the neck is not one of the recognised fat-free sites; superficial fascia there is unremarkable in fat content.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The palm of the hand has thick, fibrous-fat-padded superficial fascia to help grip, not fat-free superficial fascia.

questions.learning_objective: Name the sites where superficial fascia is devoid of fat.

questions.title: Bone type of the pisiform
questions.question: Which type of bone is the pisiform?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Long bones have two expanded ends and a shaft; the pisiform, a small nodule within a tendon, has neither.
explanations.B: Correct. The pisiform is the carpal sesamoid bone, embedded within the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris where it crosses the wrist, and it sits in the proximal carpal row alongside the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum. Being a sesamoid does not remove it from the carpus or from the eight-bone carpal count -- it is simply the one carpal bone whose shape class is "sesamoid" rather than "short", because of where it develops (within a tendon) rather than as an independent element of the row. This is the same shape-classification logic that puts the patella, the body's largest sesamoid bone, apart from the classes for long, short, flat or irregular bones.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Irregular bones, such as the vertebrae, have complex shapes with projecting processes; the pisiform's sesamoid nature is a distinct classification.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pneumatic bones contain air cavities, unlike the solid pisiform.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Flat bones are two thin compact plates around a spongy core, as in the scapula, a different structure from a sesamoid nodule in a tendon.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the pisiform as a sesamoid bone.

questions.title: What Langer's lines represent
questions.question: Thick cleavage (Langer's) lines of skin represent:

options.B: Junctional lines between superficial & deep fascia
options.C: The direction of rows of elastic fibers in the dermis
options.D: The direction of collagen fibers in the dermis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Skin creases over joints are a separate surface feature caused by repeated flexion, not the same thing as Langer's lines.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Langer's lines are not junctional lines between fascial layers; they are a purely dermal, collagen-direction phenomenon.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Elastic fibre orientation is a different structural feature from the collagen bundle direction that actually defines Langer's lines.
explanations.D: Correct. Langer's (cleavage) lines are the natural lines of tension mapped over the skin, and they run in the direction of the collagen fibre bundles of the reticular dermis. This is why surgeons plan incisions parallel to these lines wherever possible: cutting along the collagen bundle direction gaps the wound less and produces a finer scar than a cut across it. The other four options each name a different, unrelated skin feature -- none of them is what Langer's lines actually represent.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Fingerprints are epidermal ridge patterns on the fingertips, unrelated to the dermal collagen orientation that Langer's lines follow.

questions.learning_objective: State that Langer's lines follow the direction of dermal collagen fibres.

questions.title: False statement about sesamoid bones
questions.question: Regarding sesamoid bones, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:

options.B: They develop within tendons of muscles
options.C: Patella is one of its examples
options.D: They prevent obstruction of blood supply to joint
options.E: They help to reduce friction of tendon

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sesamoid bones genuinely do usually appear as small nodules, so this statement is true and is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Developing within the tendons of muscles is the defining feature of sesamoid bones, so this statement is true and is not the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The patella is the standard textbook example of a sesamoid bone, so this statement is true and is not the exception.
explanations.D: Correct. Sesamoid bones are small nodules of bone that develop within the substance of a tendon -- the patella (within the quadriceps tendon) is the largest and best-known example -- and they reduce friction on the tendon as it passes over a bony prominence, typically appearing as small rounded nodules. What they do not do is protect a joint's blood supply from obstruction; that is not a recognised function of sesamoid bones at all, and it is the false statement this EXCEPT question is built to isolate among four otherwise accurate statements.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Reducing friction on the overlying tendon is a genuine, well-recognised function of sesamoid bones, so this statement is true and is not the exception.

questions.learning_objective: Identify blood-supply protection as a false statement about sesamoid bone function.

questions.title: Location of yellow bone marrow
questions.question: In which one of the following cavities is yellow bone marrow found?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cranial cavity houses the brain, not bone marrow of either kind.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A joint cavity is the space within a synovial joint, containing synovial fluid, not bone marrow.
explanations.C: Correct. Red bone marrow is the active haemopoietic tissue of childhood, progressively replaced with age by yellow bone marrow, its inactive, fat-laden form. This replacement happens within the medullary cavity of the diaphysis -- the hollow central space of the shaft, lined by endosteum -- which is where yellow marrow is characteristically found in the adult long bones of the limbs. Recognising the medullary cavity as the site, distinct from knowing what yellow marrow itself is, is what this question adds to the red-versus-yellow marrow distinction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The epiphyseal cavity is not a standard named space; the epiphyses contain spongy, red-marrow-bearing bone, not the yellow-marrow-filled medullary cavity of the shaft.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The thoracic cavity houses the heart and lungs, not bone marrow.

questions.learning_objective: Locate yellow bone marrow within the medullary cavity.

questions.title: What the primary centre of ossification does
questions.question: Primary center of ossification of a long bone:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The metaphysis is the active region of the shaft next to the epiphyseal plate, not the location of the primary centre itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The primary centre of ossification appears before birth, in fetal life, not after birth -- secondary centres are the ones that mostly appear postnatally.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ossification of the epiphysis comes from a separate secondary centre, not from the primary centre in the shaft.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increasing the breadth (width) of the bone is the periosteum's job, not the primary centre of ossification's.
explanations.E: Correct. The primary centre of ossification is the site, usually at the middle of the future shaft, where the cartilage model of a long bone is first invaded by blood vessels and osteoblasts before birth, converting the cartilaginous shaft into bone. This event establishes the diaphysis; the epiphyses only gain their own secondary centres of ossification later, generally after birth. Naming what the primary centre actually does -- changing cartilage into bone -- is what separates this fact from simply knowing where or when it appears.

questions.learning_objective: State that the primary centre of ossification converts the cartilaginous shaft into bone.

questions.title: Plane dividing the body into anterior and posterior parts
questions.question: What is the name of the vertical plane that divides the body into anterior & posterior parts?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The median plane is vertical but divides the body into right and left halves, not anterior and posterior parts.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A right parasagittal plane still gives a right-left division (unequal in this case), not an anterior-posterior one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A left parasagittal plane also gives an unequal right-left division, not an anterior-posterior one.
explanations.D: Correct. The coronal (frontal) plane is a vertical plane that runs at right angles to the median plane, cutting the body into an anterior part towards the front and a posterior part towards the back. It is the second of the three cardinal anatomical planes, alongside the median/sagittal set (right-left division) and the transverse plane (upper-lower division). Naming a plane by the two parts it leaves behind, rather than simply by "vertical" or "horizontal", is what separates the coronal plane from the median plane -- both are vertical, but only the coronal plane gives an anterior and a posterior part.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The transverse plane divides the body into upper and lower parts, not anterior and posterior.

questions.learning_objective: Name the coronal plane as the vertical plane dividing the body into anterior and posterior parts.

questions.title: Structure never found in superficial fascia
questions.question: What is the structure that never exists in superficial fascia?

explanations.A: Correct. Superficial fascia is a layer of loose connective tissue that carries fat, cutaneous nerves, superficial blood vessels and lymphatics, and in some regions even thin skin muscles (such as the muscles of facial expression) and glands (such as the mammary gland) -- but it never contains tendons. Tendons connect muscle to bone and are found deep to the deep fascia, in continuity with the muscles they serve, not within the loose superficial layer directly under the skin. This is the one structure among the options with no place in superficial fascia at all, unlike the others, which are all normal components or contents of it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fat is a normal, often abundant, component of superficial fascia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Blood vessels, including the superficial veins, normally run within superficial fascia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cutaneous nerves are carried to the skin through superficial fascia, which conducts them from deeper structures.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Some muscles, such as the muscles of facial expression (skin muscles), do lie within superficial fascia, unlike tendons.

questions.learning_objective: State that tendons are never a component of superficial fascia.

questions.title: False statement about deep fascia
questions.question: Concerning the deep fascia, all the following are true EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Retinacula (the thickened transverse bands at the wrist and ankle) are a genuine form deep fascia takes, so this statement is true and is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fibrous flexor sheaths, which channel and support the flexor tendons, are also a true form deep fascia takes, so this is not the exception.
explanations.C: Correct. Deep fascia is a well-defined, inelastic membrane of dense collagen in the limbs and trunk, but it is characteristically absent (or only vestigial) over the face and the anterior abdominal wall -- the face instead has the thin superficial musculo-aponeurotic system associated with the muscles of expression. This is the exception the question is built around: every other statement in the list -- forming retinacula, forming fibrous flexor sheaths, covering muscles, and dividing limbs into compartments -- is a genuine, well-defined function of deep fascia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deep fascia does cover the underlying muscles as investing sheets, so this statement is true and is not the exception.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Deep fascia's intermuscular septa do divide limbs into functional compartments, so this statement is true and is not the exception.

questions.title: Bone not part of the axial skeleton
questions.question: Which one of the following is not a part of the axial skeleton?

explanations.A: Correct. The axial skeleton is the central axis of the body -- the skull, mandible, hyoid bone, sternum, ribs and vertebral column. The scapula is part of the appendicular (peripheral) skeleton, specifically the pectoral girdle, by which the upper limb attaches to the trunk; lying on the back of the thorax does not make it axial. This is the standard trap: the scapula and clavicle sit anatomically close to axial structures, but by classification they belong with the limb they serve, not with the trunk they lie against.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sternum is a true axial bone, part of the central skeletal axis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The vertebrae form the vertebral column, one of the defining components of the axial skeleton.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ribs are axial bones, attaching to the vertebral column and sternum.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The skull is axial, forming the cranial part of the body's central axis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the scapula as part of the appendicular, not axial, skeleton.

questions.title: Scapula as a flat bone
questions.question: Which one of the following is a flat bone?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The vertebra is an irregular bone because of its complex shape with projecting processes, not a flat bone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The humerus is a long bone, with two expanded ends and a shaft -- the opposite classification from a flat bone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The carpal bone is a short bone (spongy bone under a thin shell), not a flat bone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The clavicle is classified as a long bone by shape, despite its atypical double curve, not as a flat bone.
explanations.E: Correct. The scapula is a flat bone: two thin plates of compact bone with a layer of spongy bone between them, the same construction seen in the ribs and the skull cap. Its broad, blade-like shape over the posterolateral chest wall is exactly the shape this class is built to describe, distinguishing it from the long bones of the limb it is otherwise associated with (the humerus, radius and ulna). Being part of the appendicular skeleton (as the pectoral girdle) and being a "flat bone" by shape are two separate classifications that both apply to the scapula at once.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the scapula as a flat bone.

questions.title: Definition of the metaphysis
questions.question: The metaphysis of the long bone is:

options.A: The part of the epiphysis near the epiphyseal plate
options.B: The part of the epiphysis away from the epiphyseal plate
options.C: The part of the diaphysis near the epiphyseal plate
options.D: The part of the diaphysis near the center of the bone
options.E: The place of the epiphyseal plate

explanations.A: Incorrect. The metaphysis is part of the diaphysis, not part of the epiphysis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The metaphysis is part of the diaphysis, not part of the epiphysis, and it lies near the epiphyseal plate, not away from it.
explanations.C: Correct. The metaphysis is the part of the diaphysis (shaft) immediately adjacent to the epiphyseal plate -- the most metabolically active part of a growing long bone, since it is where new bone laid down at the growth plate is remodelled into mature shaft bone. It is not part of the epiphysis at all, and it lies specifically near the epiphyseal plate rather than towards the centre of the shaft, which distinguishes it from the rest of the diaphysis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The part of the diaphysis near the centre of the bone is simply the mid-shaft, distinct from the metaphysis, which lies near the epiphyseal plate.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The epiphyseal plate itself is a disc of cartilage, a separate structure from the metaphysis, which is the adjacent part of the bony shaft.

questions.learning_objective: Define the metaphysis as the part of the diaphysis nearest the epiphyseal plate.

questions.title: Long bone characteristic: medullary cavity
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of the long bone?

options.B: Its shaft has a medullary cavity
options.C: It is covered from outside by endosteum
options.D: Its metaphysis is a part of its epiphysis
options.E: Its primary center of ossification appears after birth

explanations.A: Incorrect. A long bone increases in length by its epiphyseal plates, not by the periosteum, which is instead responsible for growth in width.
explanations.B: Correct. The diaphysis (shaft) of a long bone is a tube of compact bone that surrounds a central medullary cavity, lined by endosteum and filled with bone marrow, and this hollow-shaft structure is one of the defining characteristics of a long bone. It contrasts with the epiphyses, which are spongy bone under a compact shell with no medullary cavity of their own. This same medullary cavity is the location tested elsewhere in this set as the site of yellow bone marrow.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A long bone is covered from outside by periosteum and lined from inside (the medullary cavity) by endosteum -- this statement has the two layers reversed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The metaphysis is part of the diaphysis (shaft), not part of the epiphysis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The primary centre of ossification of a long bone appears before birth, in fetal life, not after birth.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the medullary cavity within the shaft as a defining feature of a long bone.

questions.title: False statement about the skeleton of the hand
questions.question: The skeleton of the hand includes all the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Three phalanges (proximal, middle, distal) in the index finger is anatomically correct, so this statement is true and is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Five metacarpal bones, one for each digit, is anatomically correct, so this statement is true and is not the exception.
explanations.C: Correct. The carpus (wrist) is built of eight carpal bones, not seven, arranged in two rows of four: the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum and pisiform proximally, and the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate distally. Every other statement in this list about the hand skeleton is accurate -- three phalanges in the index and little fingers, five metacarpal bones, and two phalanges in the thumb -- leaving the carpal bone count as the one genuine error, the EXCEPT this question isolates.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Two phalanges (proximal and distal, with no middle phalanx) in the thumb is anatomically correct, so this statement is true and is not the exception.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Three phalanges in the little finger is anatomically correct, so this statement is true and is not the exception.

questions.learning_objective: State that the carpus has eight bones, not seven.

questions.title: Vertebra as an irregular bone
questions.question: Which one of the following is an irregular bone?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The scapula is a flat bone -- two thin plates around a spongy core -- not an irregular bone.
explanations.B: Correct. The vertebra is the standard example of an irregular bone: a complex shape with projecting processes (the spinous and transverse processes, the pedicles and laminae) that fits none of the other five shape classes, and it is built internally like a short bone, spongy bone under a thin compact shell. Its shape reflects several distinct jobs at once -- bearing load through the body, articulating through the facets, and anchoring muscles and ligaments through the processes -- which is exactly why a single simple shape class such as "long" or "flat" cannot describe it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The clavicle is classified as a long bone by shape, not as irregular.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The skull cap is a flat bone, built of outer and inner compact tables around a spongy diploe, not an irregular bone.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The patella is the classic sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon, not an irregular bone.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the vertebra as an irregular bone.

questions.title: Example of hyaline cartilage
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of haline cartilage?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The intervertebral disc is made of white fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The tip of the nose is supported by yellow elastic cartilage, not hyaline cartilage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The symphysis pubis is a fibrocartilaginous joint, made of white fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The auricle (pinna) of the ear is built of yellow elastic cartilage, not hyaline cartilage.
explanations.E: Correct. Hyaline cartilage has a translucent, glass-like matrix and is the most widespread cartilage type in the body, found at the epiphyseal plates of growing long bones, the articular surfaces of synovial joints, the costal cartilages, and the fetal skeleton before it ossifies. The epiphyseal plate is one of its classic named sites, distinguishing it from the fibrocartilage of the intervertebral discs and pubic symphysis, and from the yellow elastic cartilage of the ear and nose, each with a different matrix and a different list of sites.

questions.learning_objective: Name the epiphyseal plate as a site of hyaline cartilage.

questions.title: Bone that is part of the axial skeleton
questions.question: Axial skeleton includes:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The femur is a bone of the lower limb, part of the appendicular skeleton, not the axial skeleton.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The tibia is a bone of the lower limb, part of the appendicular skeleton, not the axial skeleton.
explanations.C: Correct. The sternum is one of the defining bones of the axial skeleton, together with the skull, hyoid, ribs and vertebral column -- it forms the anterior midline of the thoracic cage, articulating with the costal cartilages of the ribs. This is the mirror fact to the earlier question in this set asking which named bone is NOT axial (the scapula): here the sternum is squarely inside the axial group, unlike every limb or girdle bone offered as a distractor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The clavicle is part of the pectoral girdle, part of the appendicular skeleton, not the axial skeleton.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The hip bone is part of the pelvic girdle, part of the appendicular skeleton, not the axial skeleton.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the sternum as part of the axial skeleton.
